title: Removing a 'redundant' static route silently black-holes a destination
category: Hand-authored. Mechanism: recursive next-hop failure.
what_the_network_is: A 4-router mesh where one router's BGP route to a destination depends on a static route to resolve its next-hop.
the_change_made: An engineer removes that static route, believing it is redundant.
what_an_engineer_expects: Looks like cleaning up an unused route.
what_actually_happens (live ground truth: (live ground truth skipped)
why_it_matters (real-world grounding): Classic silent killer: removing the static makes the BGP next-hop unresolvable, so traffic to the destination is silently dropped (not an error — just gone).
what_it_tests_about_the_model: Whether the model follows the recursive next-hop chain (static → BGP next-hop → reachability) rather than treating the static as isolated.
how_we_verified_it / caveats: Live Batfish; deterministic. Tier A. This also covers the 'next-hop-self / recursive-resolution' class.
is_it_a_trap: no

title: Summarizing a data-center fabric blackholes half the traffic to one server
category: Hand-authored. Mechanism: DC underlay summarization hides a missing path.
what_the_network_is: A small data-center 'Clos' fabric: 2 spine switches and 3 leaf switches. One spine (spine2) has no direct path to the leaf that hosts a server.
the_change_made: An operator 'optimizes' the leaf forwarding tables by summarizing the underlay on the spines (advertise one big block instead of every subnet) and suppressing the specific server route.
what_an_engineer_expects: Looks like a pure efficiency win (smaller tables). The summary makes every spine appear to have the route, so prefix-presence checks pass.
what_actually_happens (live ground truth: (live ground truth skipped)
why_it_matters (real-world grounding): RFC 7938 warns summarization in a Clos causes blackholing. Because traffic is load-balanced across both spines, HALF the traffic to the server is silently dropped at the spine that can't reach it — while dashboards stay green.
what_it_tests_about_the_model: Whether the model catches a PARTIAL (half-of-traffic) blackhole that a simple 'is it reachable?' check misses, and sees that the summary is masking a real loss.
how_we_verified_it / caveats: Live Batfish; deterministic (scored as 'a blackhole path exists,' not which flow hashes where). Tier A, but note: this is a FIXED-asymmetry instance of the RFC 7938 hazard, not the dynamic link-failure version (that upgrade is queued).
is_it_a_trap: YES — the safe-looking answer is wrong

title: Removing one of two equal-cost paths halves redundancy (still reachable)
category: Hand-authored. Mechanism: redundancy / ECMP reduction.
what_the_network_is: A router with two equal-cost paths to a destination (for resilience).
the_change_made: One of the two equal-cost routes is removed.
what_an_engineer_expects: Reachability is completely unaffected, so a connectivity test sees nothing.
what_actually_happens (live ground truth: (live ground truth skipped)
why_it_matters (real-world grounding): Capacity/resilience is cut in half — the kind of 'nothing broke' change that removes your safety margin before the next failure.

title: Cleanup filter silently strands a customer prefix (FLAGSHIP)
category: Hand-authored flagship. Mechanism: internal routing-policy silent withdrawal.
what_the_network_is: A 3-router ISP-style network: a route reflector (r1) with two client routers (r2, r3). r3 originates a customer network (203.0.113.0/24) that has NO backup path — it is reachable only via BGP.
the_change_made: An engineer adds an outbound 'cleanup' filter on r1 toward r2 to stop advertising internal noise. The filter permits the infrastructure prefixes but, by omission, drops the customer prefix — the classic 'forgot the final permit-any.'
what_an_engineer_expects: Looks like a routine, low-risk advertisement tidy-up. The BGP session stays up and the loopbacks are still advertised, so the network 'looks fine.'
what_actually_happens (live ground truth: (live ground truth skipped)
why_it_matters (real-world grounding): This is the single most common shape of change-induced outage (the 'implicit deny-all' maintenance trap; the prefix-level shape of the Facebook Oct-2021 outage).
what_it_tests_about_the_model: Whether the model knows a policy edit can strand a prefix WITHOUT dropping the session — i.e. it does not reflexively predict a session loss, and it does catch the silent withdrawal.
how_we_verified_it / caveats: Ground truth computed live by Batfish; deterministic. Tier A (faithful minimal instance).
is_it_a_trap: YES — the safe-looking answer is wrong

title: Dropping specific routes while a summary route survives (reachable, but TE broken)
category: Hand-authored. Mechanism: aggregate masks the loss of more-specifics.
what_the_network_is: A network advertising both a summary route (a /24) and more-specific routes (two /25s) that pin traffic for traffic-engineering reasons.
the_change_made: The cleanup filter drops the two specific /25 routes but keeps the covering /24 summary.
what_an_engineer_expects: Coarse reachability still works (the /24 covers everything), so a ping test passes and it looks fine.
what_actually_happens (live ground truth: (live ground truth skipped)
why_it_matters (real-world grounding): A pernicious real trap: reachability survives, but the traffic-engineering/multihoming the specifics provided is silently broken (RFC 4632 de-aggregation pitfall).
what_it_tests_about_the_model: Whether the model sees that 'still reachable' is NOT 'still correct' — it must flag that the specific routes are gone AND that the design intent they served is violated, even though no destination became unreachable.
how_we_verified_it / caveats: Live Batfish; deterministic. Tier A. This is the case that justifies a first-class 'intent' dimension.
is_it_a_trap: YES — the safe-looking answer is wrong

category: Hand-authored. Mechanism: the same withdrawal, applied fabric-wide.
what_the_network_is: A larger route reflector with several client routers, all serving the same customer prefix.
the_change_made: The same cleanup filter, but applied as a template to every client at once (how operators actually roll out policy).
what_an_engineer_expects: Same 'routine cleanup' expectation — but now the mistake is replicated everywhere.

title: Same filter, but a static backup hides the damage (the discriminator)
category: Hand-authored. Mechanism: same withdrawal, but control-plane-only.
what_the_network_is: Identical to the flagship, except client r2 ALSO has a static backup route to the customer prefix.
the_change_made: The same outbound cleanup filter on r1 toward r2.

what_actually_happens (live ground truth: (live ground truth skipped)

title: A more-specific route leak pulls traffic into a black hole (a route is ADDED, nothing is lost)
category: Hand-authored. Mechanism: route leak / longest-prefix-match hijack.
what_the_network_is: Three networks (autonomous systems) in a chain: a victim that owns a prefix, a transit in the middle, and a 'leaker.'
the_change_made: The leaker starts advertising a MORE-SPECIFIC piece of the victim's address space (a /25 of the victim's /24) that it cannot actually deliver.
what_an_engineer_expects: A change that only ADDS a route looks harmless — no session drops, no route is lost; a 'count what disappeared' view sees nothing.
what_actually_happens (live ground truth: (live ground truth skipped)
why_it_matters (real-world grounding): This is the Cloudflare-2019 / Telekom-Malaysia-2015 mechanism: longest-prefix-match pulls the victim's traffic to the leaker, where it is dropped. Session and prefix counts give zero signal.
what_it_tests_about_the_model: The core argument for multi-dimensional scoring: whether the model sees that adding a route can cause a blackhole — the damage is purely in the data plane.
how_we_verified_it / caveats: Live Batfish; deterministic. Tier A. (We model the leaker's no-path as a discard/blackhole — the worst case; the real incident was congestion-based degradation.)
is_it_a_trap: YES — the safe-looking answer is wrong

title: A LOCAL_PREF tweak reroutes traffic off a mandatory inspection node
category: Hand-authored. Mechanism: BGP attribute change shifts the path.
what_the_network_is: An internal network where traffic to a customer must pass through an inspection node ('way'); there is also a bypass path ('alt').
the_change_made: An engineer raises the LOCAL_PREF on the bypass path (a one-line attribute edit, e.g. for cost reasons).
what_an_engineer_expects: Tempting wrong answer: 'changing BGP config will drop a session.' It won't — and the destination stays perfectly reachable.
what_actually_happens (live ground truth: (live ground truth skipped)
why_it_matters (real-world grounding): The documented LLM failure mode (models wrongly predict a session drop on an attribute change). The real harm is a security/compliance one: traffic now bypasses the inspection node while everything still pings.
what_it_tests_about_the_model: Whether the model avoids the session-loss reflex AND catches the second-order effect (a required waypoint is now skipped), with no reachability loss to tip it off.
how_we_verified_it / caveats: Live Batfish; deterministic. Tier B — the iBGP next-hop is resolved with static routes (a Batfish modeling workaround), which is non-idiomatic; an eBGP idiomatic twin is queued.

title: A cleanup locks the NOC out of a device — zero customer prefixes touched
category: Hand-authored. Mechanism: management-plane / out-of-band lockout.
what_the_network_is: A network with a normal customer data path AND a NOC 'jump host' that reaches each device's management address over the network (in-band management).
the_change_made: A cleanup filter on the core router omits the device management subnet when advertising toward the jump host (again, by omission).
what_an_engineer_expects: The tempting wrong answer: 'no customer prefixes are affected, so this is safe.' That conclusion is exactly backwards.
what_actually_happens (live ground truth: (live ground truth skipped)
why_it_matters (real-world grounding): This is the recovery-path failure in Facebook-2021, AWS-2021, Rogers-2022, Cloudflare-2022: the change severs the tools you need to fix it. Zero customer impact, top severity.
what_it_tests_about_the_model: Whether the model recognizes that breaking the management path is catastrophic even though no customer route changed — inverted-severity reasoning.
how_we_verified_it / caveats: Live Batfish; deterministic. Tier A. NOTE: built but NOT yet through the noc-veteran/red-team review gate.

title: De-aggregation floods a router past its forwarding-table limit
category: Hand-authored. Mechanism: scale / FIB-TCAM overflow.
what_the_network_is: An edge router that learns a single summary route (a /16) from upstream and has a limited forwarding-table budget.
the_change_made: Upstream removes the summary and instead advertises all the constituent more-specific routes (de-aggregation), multiplying the route count the edge must install.
what_an_engineer_expects: Again a change that only ADDS routes — nothing is withdrawn, so a 'count what's lost' view sees nothing.
what_actually_happens (live ground truth: (live ground truth skipped)
why_it_matters (real-world grounding): This is the Rogers-2022 / '512k day' mechanism: the device's forwarding hardware (e.g. TCAM) overflows its capacity, after which behavior is undefined. Routers crash or silently drop.
what_it_tests_about_the_model: Whether the model reasons about a RESOURCE limit (counts the routes vs the device's budget) rather than just connectivity — a different axis entirely.
how_we_verified_it / caveats: Live Batfish gives the route count; the capacity limit is a stated spec annotation. Tier D (spec-annotated) — we score 'does it cross the budget,' not which routes get evicted (hardware-dependent).
is_it_a_trap: YES — the safe-looking answer is wrong

the_change_made: A static route on the source is changed so traffic takes the alternate path instead.

Upstream de-aggregates a summary into many more-specific routes so the installed route count stays UNDER the budget — no overflow (a trap for models that pattern-match 'de-aggregation = overflow'), while the covering summary stays advertised (reachability is fine; this is pure forwarding-table pressure). Budget magnitudes are anchored to public hardware ceilings (e.g. the 16,384-entry ECMP-group table), scaled down.
what_an_engineer_expects: A routine, safe-looking change.
what_actually_happens (live ground truth: (intended structure as described in 'the_change_made'; verified live against Batfish at sweep time — all 60 instances 10×-determinism-gated)
why_it_matters (real-world grounding): Mass-produced with randomized addressing/ASNs so models can't win by memorizing a public incident — the contamination-controlled split.
what_it_tests_about_the_model: The same mechanism reasoning at scale on never-before-seen numbering.
how_we_verified_it / caveats: Generator deterministic per seed; full suite 10×-determinism-gated. Tier A.
is_it_a_trap: YES — the safe-looking answer is wrong
